ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the figure is a height contour map of the 3°C isothermal surface, and the contour values generally increase from left to right and from the lower left to the right side. ① is located near the low-value closed line in the upper left, close to 3000 m, and is the position with the lowest height among the four points; ② is near the 3200 m contour line; ③ is located near 3300 m, with a 3400 m contour line beside it; ④ is located near the closed line on the right side, close to 3500 m. Then reason: the near-surface terrain is low and flat and the temperature is the same at 21.5°C, while the temperature of the 3°C isothermal surface is fixed at 3°C, so the temperature difference from the ground to this isothermal surface is uniformly 21.5−3=18.5°C. The vertical temperature lapse rate can be estimated as Γ=18.5°C/the height of the local 3°C isothermal surface. The smaller the height, the larger Γ is, the more unstable the atmosphere is, and the more easily the airplane feels turbulence. Among the four points, the height of the 3°C isothermal surface at ① is the smallest, therefore the vertical temperature lapse rate is the largest, and the turbulence is the strongest.

method.method_draft: First describe the contour map: identify which height contour each numbered point lies on or closest to. Use the text-given near-surface temperature 21.5°C and the isothermal-surface temperature 3°C, so the vertical temperature difference is fixed at 18.5°C. For each point estimate Γ=(21.5−3)/height-to-3°C-surface. Since ① has the smallest height of the 3°C surface, its Γ is the largest, so turbulence is strongest there. Answer ①.
